body: Canada uses British English spelling (e.g., colour, centre) and the metric system (e.g., kilometres). This is a key difference from the US, which uses American English and the imperial system (e.g., miles).
Generation 2 coverage, identifiable by its large circular car blur and sky halo, is common in rural Canada. This is a strong clue for Canada as it's very rare in the US.
Canada has Generation 4 'smallcam' coverage, which has a low-mounted camera and a large circular blur, sometimes with a visible mirror on the right.
Canada is the only country that uses unique diamond-shaped T-intersection signs with a checkerboard pattern. This is a very strong clue for Canada, as the US uses rectangular signs.
Canadian speed limit signs use the word 'MAXIMUM' and show speeds in km/h, resulting in higher numbers than in the US. US signs use 'SPEED LIMIT' and mph.
Canadian roads often feature a single yellow centre line, although double yellow lines are also seen. Double yellow lines are more common in the US, so this can be a helpful but not definitive clue.
Communal mailboxes are a feature of Canada and are rare in the US. Additionally, Canada Post has a red logo, while the US Postal Service logo is blue.
Canadian road signs are often less wordy than in the US. For instance, yield and railroad crossing signs in Canada are typically symbol-only, whereas US signs include text.
Each Canadian province has a unique licence plate design, and several provinces do not require front plates. This can be a useful clue for regional identification.
The French language is a strong indicator for Québec and parts of New Brunswick. Bilingual signs can also be found elsewhere in Canada due to its status as an official language.
Each province has unique highway shields, but the green Trans-Canada Highway shield is consistent across all ten provinces.
Provinces have unique kilometre markers. A notable example is in Ontario, where markers have a distinctive white square at the bottom.
Provinces have unique speed limit signs; Ontario's may have a black bar at the bottom, British Columbia's include 'km/h' without the bar, and Québec's may be in French.
Alberta has a unique and common cylindrical black and white bollard with two black bands. Variations with yellow, blue, or green bands can also be found.
Manitoba uses black and grey bollards, often with an orange stripe. A simpler version with just a black top is shared with Saskatchewan.
British Columbia features thin, slightly curved black-and-white bollards, which are distinct from the thicker, cylindrical Alberta bollards.
Québec has unique long, thin white bollards with a red or green reflector, which are always attached to guardrails.
Yellow fire hydrant markers on signposts are a strong clue for Québec. Variations in color and design can indicate specific cities like Québec City or Trois-Rivières.
Rectangular markers of various colours on the side of the road are a good indicator for Québec.
Diamond-shaped markers of various colours on the side of the road are a good indicator for Ontario.
Ontario often features guardrails with cylindrical wooden posts connected by exactly three metal wires.
Flat, yellow bollards are a feature of the Trans-Canada highway in New Brunswick.
The Northwest Territories has a black and white cylindrical bollard with two thick black bands, distinguishing it from the similar Alberta bollard which has thinner bands.
In British Columbia and New Brunswick, pole transformers face the road, whereas in other provinces they are parallel to the wires.
Transformers in Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia are installed at a 45° angle. PEI poles often have red numbers on the side.
A distinctive poletop with two side insulators and one top insulator is a strong clue for Ontario.
Québec poles can sometimes be identified by poletops with insulator rods that are angled slightly upwards.
A vertical black and yellow label on a utility pole, containing a small 'Q', is a unique marker for Québec.
Utility poles in Prince Edward Island can often be identified by a small white sticker.
Saskatchewan features a unique pattern of alternating pole top insulators, where the arrangement swaps on consecutive poles.
Unlike the rest of Canada, Québec's diamond-shaped T-intersection signs do not have a checkerboard pattern.
Newfoundland's T-intersection signs are unique for having a rectangular yellow border around the standard diamond shape.
Road signs with green backsides are a strong indicator for British Columbia, and are also sometimes seen on Prince Edward Island.
In British Columbia, road signs may be hung down from unique T-shaped signposts.
British Columbia heavily favors the use of concrete barriers over traditional guardrails on its highways.
